text: The lifeboat station kept a service book, and the rescue on the outer bar takes up three lines of it. “Heavy sea. Eleven saved from the schooner. Boat stove in.” The coxswain who wrote those lines had been out for nine hours.
strengths: tells the listener what kind of document it is before reading from it
lets the record's flat style speak for itself
the closing fact recolours the quotation without explaining it
weaknesses: the clipped style belongs to the record, and the narration must not borrow it outside the quotation marks
three lines, eleven saved and nine hours are as many numbers as a passage this short can carry
spokenRhythm: A medium sentence of set-up, three clipped phrases in the record's own voice, and a plain full sentence that lands after them.
narrativeFunction: Gives the rescue in the words of the man who led it, then adds the one fact his words leave out.
whyItWorks: The narration names the source and its brevity, then steps aside for the quotation. It does not comment on the understatement. It adds one fact the coxswain didn't write down, and the listener hears the distance between three lines and nine hours without being told to. The narrator's own sentences stay whole, so the clipped phrases are clearly the record speaking.

text: In his second winter at the trading post, the clerk Andrew Moss wrote to the company asking for a transfer. The letter is polite and very short. “I have now gone eleven weeks without speaking to anyone who was not selling me a fur.” The company sent him another ledger.
strengths: sets up who wrote, when and why in a single sentence
the company's answer is given as a fact and left alone
weaknesses: The letter is polite and very short edges towards describing a document the picture may already show
spokenRhythm: A long sentence of set-up, a short one about the letter, the quotation, and a short dry close.
narrativeFunction: Lets a clerk describe his isolation in his own words and shows how the company answered him.
whyItWorks: The narration gives the listener only what they need to hear the quotation properly, then gets out of the way. The clerk's own sentence is funnier and sadder than any description of loneliness, and the last line answers it with a fact instead of a comment. Nobody is told how to feel about the ledger.

text: The inquiry's clerk took down the evidence in shorthand and wrote it out fair the next morning, so what survives is his version of what the witnesses said. A mill hand named Sarah Pike was asked why she had not left the building when the bell rang. “Because it rang every day, sir, and the overseer docked us if we stopped.”
strengths: says how the words came down to us before quoting them
the question is reported so the answer can stand alone
ends on the witness, not on the narrator
weaknesses: the opening sentence is long and carries two steps in the record's history
the caveat is worth making once per film, not before every quotation from the inquiry
spokenRhythm: A long sentence about the record, a medium sentence that puts the question, and the witness's answer to close.
narrativeFunction: Explains why the workers stayed inside, in the words of one of them, and is honest about how those words survive.
whyItWorks: The caveat about the clerk's version is said the way a curious person would say it, and it costs one clause. The narration then reports the question in plain words so the answer needs no introduction. Ending on her reply leaves the cause of the disaster in a worker's mouth, where it carries more weight than a summary would. It is good rather than excellent because the first sentence is heavy.

text: The underwriters who met at the coffee house signed their names under each risk they took on, and now and then one of them added a word or two beside it. Against a brig sailing north late in the season, one underwriter wrote, “At this premium and not a penny less.” The brig came home in the spring, and he kept every penny.
strengths: explains the practice before giving the example
the quotation is short enough to be heard whole
the last line calls back to the quotation's own words
weaknesses: the first sentence carries both the practice and the habit of adding notes
the penny callback is neat enough that the listener can hear it being made, so it should not be used again in the same sequence
spokenRhythm: A long explanatory sentence, a medium one that delivers the quotation at its end, and a shorter close that echoes it.
narrativeFunction: Shows how underwriters priced a risk through one man's note, and how the bet paid him.
whyItWorks: The first sentence teaches the listener how to read the note before they hear it, so the quotation needs no comment. The ending says what happened and borrows the underwriter's own phrase, so the payoff comes out of the record rather than the narrator. It is good rather than excellent because the opening is heavy and the callback is a little too tidy.

text: The expedition's official report says the men were in good spirits throughout the winter. The surgeon kept a diary of his own. His entry for the middle of January reads, in full, “Played cards. Nobody spoke.”
strengths: two sources are set side by side and the narrator takes no side aloud
in full tells the listener the brevity is the point
weaknesses: it works only if the film does not go on to explain what the entry means
spokenRhythm: Two plain sentences that set up the two sources, then a medium one that ends on four words from the diary.
narrativeFunction: Undercuts the official account of the winter with a single private record.
whyItWorks: The narration reports what each source says and stops. The contradiction is the listener's discovery, and in full is the only nudge it allows itself. The surgeon's four words carry the mood of that winter better than any description of despair.

text: The story in the town is that when the railway company offered to buy Ellen Marsh's orchard, she told its agent, “Not while I'm standing in it.” The company's minutes record her answer as a price, and a high one. Both may be true.
strengths: the quotation is credited to the town's story, not to the record
the minutes are set beside it as a competing source
the last line leaves room for both without a lecture
weaknesses: Ellen Marsh is introduced through the company's offer rather than her own work
the listener will want to hear the price soon after
spokenRhythm: A long sentence that carries the story and the quotation, a medium one for the record, and a four-word close.
narrativeFunction: Gives a remembered line its due while showing what the documents say she actually did.
whyItWorks: The quotation is framed as a story the town tells, so the narration never claims she said it. The minutes are set beside it without a debunking, and the dry last line suggests a woman shrewd enough to have said both. It is good rather than excellent because the quotation is doing the work of introducing her.
